1. The animation shows a grid of many houses. Each house stands for one historical scenario, and the scenarios use US home prices (FHFA), rents (BLS) and mortgage rates (Freddie Mac). A house is lit if the buyer came out ahead after ten years. It stays dark if the renter came out ahead. The labels say it is "ILLUSTRATIVE", "US only" and "history, not a forecast".

2. At first every house is dark. The houses then light up, starting at the front-left corner and spreading toward the back and right. By frames 4 to 6, most of the grid is lit. A band of dark houses remains along the far right and back edge, and it shrinks a little by frame 6.

3. In most of the historical scenarios, the buyer ended up ahead of the renter after ten years. In a minority of them, the renter did better. So buying has usually beaten renting over a ten-year hold, but not always.

4. A viewer might take away that buying has historically paid off more often than not if you stay about ten years. They might also take away that it isn't guaranteed, since some starting conditions favored renting. The animation does not give a firm recommendation.

5. The takeaway in 4 is my own reading. The on-screen text only defines what lit and dark mean and says "history, not a forecast". It gives no advice. The animation also doesn't say what share of scenarios were lit, so "most" is my estimate from the picture.
